entities.summary:
The Fellowship of the Ring, published in 1954, is the first volume of J.R.R. Tolkien's epic fantasy saga, The Lord of the Rings. Set in the mythical world of Middle-earth, this narrative centers around a diverse group of characters united to destroy the One Ring, a symbol of ultimate power and corruption created by the dark lord Sauron. Tolkien, a philologist and professor at Oxford, crafted this narrative against the backdrop of the post-World War II era, reflecting the anxieties and hopes of a world emerging from conflict. The Fellowship includes iconic figures such as Frodo Baggins, Gandalf, and Aragorn, representing various races and cultures within Middle-earth, all of whom are drawn together by the common purpose of thwarting Sauron’s ambitions.

The narrative unfolds across several regions of Middle-earth, notably the Shire, Rivendell, and the Mines of Moria, as the Fellowship embarks on a perilous journey filled with trials and tribulations. Key events include the Council of Elrond, where the Fellowship is formed, and the encounter with the Balrog in Moria, which led to Gandalf's fall. The book intricately weaves themes of friendship, sacrifice, and the struggle against evil, encapsulated in moments that resonate deeply with readers. The Fellowship's journey is not merely physical; it is also a profound exploration of moral and ethical dilemmas faced by its members, each representing different aspects of humanity's virtues and vices.
